title: Yup The Poems at Sin É

author: ella
body:
On May 17th, poet Conor Killeen hosted his first headline show “Yup The Poems” at Sin É in Dublin. Joining him on stage throughout the night were Adam Kelly, Rory O’Mahony, and Eva Mary Lucy, with the night being hosted by Ned Dunn. This was the first poetry performance event I had attended, so I came in with few expectations of how such an event should run. The atmosphere in the packed Sin É basement was upbeat and cheerful, and throughout the night the poets on stage consistently voiced support and praise for one another, with each opener celebrating this milestone event for Killeen. The poetry community of Dublin certainly made a good first impression on me; their warmth towards one another ran through the whole event. 

Ned Dunn opened the event, dubbing himself the “sacrificial poet” of the night. His poem, ‘The Tragedy of Christy Ó Súilleabháin,’ spoke of love and religion with lines such as “her religion was her own, not one of inheritance" and “we shall love ourselves despite our own familiar failures” standing out to me as emblematic of the poem’s central themes. What struck me most was how much each poet really inhabited the poems they performed. Each sentence and phrase seemed to transport the poet and by extension the audience to the place and time in which the event first occurred. While true of all the poets who performed throughout the night, this is perhaps especially true of Dunn, whose emotive rendering of the poem seemed to occupy space in the room itself.

Following Dunn’s introductory performance was Adam Kelly, founder of the Smithfield Creatives. Kelly’s poetry, even when comedic in parts, didn’t shy away from uncomfortable subjects, examining the Irish relationship towards drinking in his first two poems ‘Double Duck Szechuan’ and ‘Uisce Bheatha’. The most powerful poem by far was about the poet’s grandmother’s battle with dementia. Kelly here expertly struck the balance between the profound sadness associated with the disease and the mundanity of daily life, exacerbated by the slow decline associated with the illness. “It was a slow process, which in a way made it harder to digest” explains the unique loss experienced by family members of those with dementia. The line “Is that your car outside?” was repeated throughout, exemplifying the impossibility of forward progression. Even as time passed within the narrative of the poem, the same line is repeated, the same question asked. 

Kelly’s penultimate poem, ‘Crane,’ was about the intersection between culture and infrastructure in Dublin. Kelly addresses the belief that “a lot of cranes in the city is a sign of prosperity,” claiming that rapid development was “knocking down our identity” to make space for “hotel after hotel after hotel.” The poem echoed a sentiment that can be heard expressed by many Dublin residents in recent years and months, with an increasing number of protests across the city arguing against the destruction of sites of cultural importance. Only this week, activists from the Revolutionary Housing League have occupied a long-abandoned pub in the Liberties to establish the Anne Devlin Community Centre. Kelly’s poem speaks to this vocal demand for creative spaces. Kelly finished with a poem called ‘Fledgling,’ spoken to music by Geo Postal, a Dublin-based post-rock band.

Next on stage was Rory O’Mahony, whose poetry defies easy definition. His opening poem ‘When I Lived in a Wallet’ tells the story of a coin who travels around an increasingly technological world, watching itself become redundant in the face of digital transactions. My favourite poem of his was ‘An Ode to Easons,’ which detailed the poet’s search for a copybook with “pages made to measure,” among other stationery items. I particularly liked the line: “I got a multicoloured pen; I choose blue all the time,” which seems to me to demonstrate the unique quality of O’Mahony’s writing. Amidst the slight absurdity of his topics is a commentary on modern-day life. Situated between a call-and-response of “You say ‘Ballymawhat?’ I say ‘Ballymaloe’” is the line “it’s very easy to believe things when they’re put in front of you.” O’Mahony’s poetry pushes the listener to fight against a surface-level interpretation, both of his poetry and of your own life.

O’Mahony’s performance was measured and even-toned. Especially towards the end of his set, he spoke almost as though winding up to the punchline in a joke, a constant comic undercurrent running through his performance. His final poem was rapidly spoken and painted the picture of “a disgusted-at-the-sun-for-being-warm kind of guy.” Despite my inability to neatly categorise O'Mahony's performance style, it was one which I enjoyed immensely. When Dunn returned to the stage following O’Mahony’s performance, he described the poet as someone who “embodies the balance between whimsy and poetry” which I feel perfectly sums up the tone of O’Mahony’s performance. 

Eva Mary Lucy, 2025 All-Ireland Slam Champion, closed off the opening half of the evening. To listen to Lucy was to be transported with her to the time and place in which the event of the poem took place. Her profiles of the family members she discussed were expertly rendered; in only a few lines she was able to give a whole image of a person and seemed to bring them to life on the stage. ‘Womanhood’ was a poem about the poet’s mother and her struggle with cancer, and asked the question “What made her a woman after it was all taken away?” The poem dispelled the notion that what it means to be a woman can only be found in the body, and described the “courage in excess” of the poet’s mother. Lucy gave a dynamic performance, lowering and raising her voice as the tone of her poems changed. She made full use of the space available to her, gesturing and miming certain acts to emphasise the words she spoke. Words themselves seemed to take on a shape through Lucy’s performance.

My favourite poem of Lucy’s was entitled ‘The Finest Days,’ which detailed the physical presence of grief experienced after her father’s death. The emptiness of the “shirts that once held your shape” were a poignant image of loss, the reminder of what is no longer there standing out amidst what is left behind. The poem, while sad, was full of love and evidently happy memories of the poet’s time with her father. In reaching in to one of his coat pockets, she finds a hair clip she had worn as a child, picked up and kept safe by her father. The image of the hair clip prompts the closing line of the poem: “love like yours, it doesn’t end, it just changes hands.” Lucy’s final poems of the evening turned towards romantic love and struggling with disordered eating. One poem dealt with the expectation versus reality of entering into a romantic relationship, likened to opening her grandmother’s biscuit tin and finding sewing needles and thread instead. Still, “your lack of biscuits took me by surprise.”

‘Pie/Pi’ spoke of a “little me” who “always loved numbers,” for whom the thoughts of “what to consume became all-consuming, and losing felt like winning.” The closing line of the poem “I deserve to take up space” seemed to me to speak to the very nature of performance. Each of these poets were unafraid to take up space in the room, allowing their words to fill the space we shared that evening. The power of poetry was a recurring theme, for none more than the headliner Conor Killeen, who appeared onstage after a short interval.

Dunn’s introduction claimed that Killeen “only started poetry about a year ago,” a feat made even more impressive by the genuine vulnerability and emotion displayed by Killeen onstage. In a video which played before Killeen’s entrance, the poet discussed having experienced poor mental health and detailed how poems were “where the real healing lay.” He spoke of his fourteen-year-old self who wrote his first poem while coming to terms with being gay and how all the poems he writes today are in some way addressed to that version of himself. Killeen’s first poem of the evening spoke of the importance of community in an increasingly unaffordable Dublin. “It’s a horrible country in which to be sad,” he said of an Ireland in which “the stairs keep moving further away.”

The following poem ‘I’m A Kid Again’ spoke of his childhood desire to “get an extra hour away from the house” and juxtaposed childhood games with the violence experienced at home. What was special about this performance was the soundscape created by Killeen; feet running up the stairs, the sound of a slap. Coupled with the intensity of the emotion within the lines, this made for a truly immersive performance. The poem expertly demonstrated the feeling of being trapped in an inescapable place and time, and the power of memory to transport you back to this place unbidden. 

The next poem, about a close friend’s death, built in speed and tension through the poet’s performance. A theme that was raised for the first time in this poem, but which would remain relevant for the remainder of Killeen’s set, was the power of the mind to inflict pain upon itself. Killeen speaks here of when your “own thoughts hate you,” and having to push past the rising tension to the aftermath, wherein the poet decides: “I deserve to see life when I’m older, bolder and sober.” Moving into ‘Memories,’ this sense of the mind and thoughts exerting control over the self develops, and this poem sees writing as the means through which control can be reasserted.

Killeen’s poetry depicts the power of the mind to be unseen and unheard by those around you. In ‘Little Ball of Feathers’ the poet is “being battered at the hands of [his] thoughts.” This physical description of harm makes evident the difficulty of having mental health troubles be recognised by others, as the mind attacking you in a place that no one else can see. Poetry, particularly the performance of poetry, renders this particular power useless, and destabilises the hold that mental illness can have on those who suffer from it by putting thoughts to words and speaking them out loud. A common theme in Killeen’s poetry was dissecting ideas of performance itself, breaking down the carefully delineated boundary between what happens in the mind and how a person presents themselves. The poet encouraged the crowd to talk to those around them, and not to attempt to “stop anyone from getting in.”  Killeen’s poems fracture this inside-outside boundary, bringing his thoughts and feelings of the past crashing through to the present where their presence is certainly felt. Killeen’s poetry can be seen as an instruction manual for breaking out of destructive thinking. 

Before his final poem, the eponymous ‘Yup The Poems,’ Killeen thanked a wide range of people from the Dublin poetry community for their support. ‘Yup The Poems’ epitomises the themes discussed throughout this article, speaking of how poetry offers an avenue for thoughts trapped inside the mind to be pushed out: “things inside poured into these lines.” Killeen ended the poem with the phrase: “every poet has a story they hold inside.”

Killeen was an arresting speaker, giving new meaning to his poetry through the performance. To watch Killeen speak felt as though he was re-experiencing every emotion detailed in his poems onstage, and this emotion was certainly felt by those in the room. For all the poets who performed on the night, their passion and enthusiasm came through very clearly, and made for an enjoyable evening for all those who attended.
